overview.title: Word-level vocabulary and testing the character tokenizer on Moby Dick
overview.main_topic: Finishing WordTokenizer, computing a word vocabulary (Listing 14.4), downloading Moby Dick, and inspecting the resulting character vocabulary and the character-level length of the novel's first line
overview.central_idea: Swapping the word regex into the vocabulary function gives compute_word_vocabulary. On real text, the full Moby Dick, the character tokenizer needs only 64 vocabulary entries, even with a cap of 100, ordered by frequency from space and "e" down to rare symbols like "<" and ">". But it encodes the 63-character opening sentence as 63 tokens, one per character, which sets up the comparison with the word tokenizer on p.414.
overview.importance: This is the first time the hand-built tokenizers meet a real corpus, and the measurements here (vocabulary length, sequence length) are the evidence for the character vs. word trade-off that motivates subword tokenization in 14.2.2.
learning_objectives: Read Listing 14.4 and relate it to Listing 14.2
Use keras.utils.get_file to download a text corpus and read it as a list of lines
Interpret the vocabulary length (64) and why it is below max_size=100
Explain the frequency order visible in the first and last vocabulary entries
Explain why the character-level encoding of the opening line has length 63

summary:
The page first completes **Listing 14.3**: `WordTokenizer.__call__` ends with `indices = self.index(tokens)` and `return indices`, exactly like CharTokenizer.

Next, the new split rule is substituted into the vocabulary function. **Listing 14.4, `compute_word_vocabulary(inputs, max_size)`**, is Listing 14.2 with a word Counter and `re.findall(r"[\w]+|[.,!?;]", x)` in place of the character regex. It lowercases, counts, puts `[UNK]` first, keeps the `max_size - 1` most common words and returns a token -> index dict.

The authors then try both tokenizers on **real-world input: the full text of *Moby Dick* by Herman Melville**. They import `keras`, download the Project Gutenberg file with `keras.utils.get_file(origin="https://www.gutenberg.org/files/2701/old/moby10b.txt")`, read it as a list of lines (`list(open(filename, "r"))`), compute a character vocabulary with `max_size=100`, and build `char_tokenizer = CharTokenizer(vocabulary)`.

Inspecting the results:

- **Vocabulary length: 64**. The whole novel, lowercased, contains only 63 distinct characters (excluding newlines), so the cap of 100 is never reached.
- **Vocabulary start**: `["[UNK]", " ", "e", "t", "a", "o", "n", "i", "s", "h"]`. After `[UNK]`, the entries are in descending frequency: space first, then the familiar English letter-frequency order e, t, a, o, n, i, s, h.
- **Vocabulary end**: `["@", "$", "%", "#", "=", "~", "&", "+", "<", ">"]`. These are the rarest symbols, likely mostly from the Gutenberg license text and markup.
- **Line length: 63** for "Call me Ishmael. Some years ago--never mind how long precisely.", one index per character.

The page ends with "Now what about the word-level tokenizer?", answered on p.414.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The authors print the vocabulary length (64), its first ten keys ([UNK], space, e, t, a, o, n, i, s, h), its last ten keys (@ $ % # = ~ & + < >), and the encoded length of the novel's first sentence (63).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Python dicts preserve insertion order, so list(vocabulary.keys()) lists tokens by frequency rank. The top looks like standard English letter frequency; the bottom is rare symbols. 64 < 100 means the cap did not bind: lowercase Moby Dick only uses 63 distinct non-newline characters. A 63-character sentence encodes to 63 indices because each character is one token.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is half of the comparison on p.414: the character tokenizer covers the entire book with a tiny vocabulary (64), but every input becomes a very long sequence.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: because the vocabulary covers every character in the training text, CharTokenizer will produce [UNK] only for characters never seen in Moby Dick (e.g. accented letters or emoji).

concepts.name: Word-level vocabulary
concepts.definition: A vocabulary computed by counting word-and-punctuation tokens and keeping the max_size - 1 most common plus [UNK].
concepts.intuition: Same recipe as for characters, but the ingredients are words.
concepts.technical: Listing 14.4 = Listing 14.2 with the regex [\w]+|[.,!?;]. Word vocabularies grow much faster than character ones, so the cap matters (p.414: 2,000 fills quickly; about 17,000 needed for the whole book).
concepts.significance: Needed for WordTokenizer; its size trades coverage against parameters.
concepts.example: compute_word_vocabulary(["The cat. The dog."], 4) -> {[UNK]:0, the:1, .:2, cat:3}.
concepts.misconception: Unlike the character case, a word vocabulary capped at a few thousand does not cover all of a book.

concepts.name: Character tokenization on real text
concepts.definition: Measured on Moby Dick: 64 vocabulary entries cover everything; a 63-character sentence becomes 63 tokens.
concepts.technical: Sequence length = number of non-newline characters; vocabulary = distinct characters + [UNK], ordered by frequency.
concepts.significance: Provides the numbers for the trade-off discussed on p.414.
concepts.example: "Call me Ishmael. Some years ago--never mind how long precisely." -> 63 indices.
concepts.misconception: A small vocabulary does not mean a cheap model overall: long sequences raise compute for sequence models.

concepts.name: Frequency-ordered vocabulary
concepts.definition: In these vocabularies, index order is frequency rank because tokens are appended from most_common.
concepts.intuition: Index 1 is the most common token, the highest index the rarest kept one.
concepts.technical: dict insertion order (Python 3.7+) preserves the order of enumerate(vocabulary), so keys()[:10] are the top tokens and keys()[-10:] the rarest.
concepts.significance: Lets you read corpus statistics off the vocabulary; Keras' TextVectorization also orders by frequency.
concepts.example: Space is the most frequent character, then e, t, a, o, n, i, s, h.
concepts.misconception: Not in the book: the trailing symbols (@, $, %, #, ...) probably come from the Project Gutenberg header and license text rather than from Melville's prose.

code.title: Downloading Moby Dick and building a character tokenizer
code.original_code:
import keras

filename = keras.utils.get_file(
    origin="https://www.gutenberg.org/files/2701/old/moby10b.txt",
)
moby_dick = list(open(filename, "r"))

vocabulary = compute_char_vocabulary(moby_dick, max_size=100)
char_tokenizer = CharTokenizer(vocabulary)
code.what_it_does: Downloads the Gutenberg text of Moby Dick, reads it into a list of lines, computes a character vocabulary capped at 100 entries and instantiates a CharTokenizer with it.

line_explanations.explanation: Imports Keras for its file-download utility.
get_file downloads the URL (once; cached afterwards) and returns the local path. With only origin given, the file name is taken from the URL.
Opens the file in text mode and materializes its lines as a list of strings.
Builds the frequency-ordered character vocabulary (Listing 14.2) with at most 100 entries.
Creates the tokenizer of Listing 14.1 bound to that vocabulary.

>>> print("Vocabulary length:", len(vocabulary))
Vocabulary length: 64
>>> print("Vocabulary start:", list(vocabulary.keys())[:10])
Vocabulary start: ["[UNK]", " ", "e", "t", "a", "o", "n", "i", "s", "h"]
>>> print("Vocabulary end:", list(vocabulary.keys())[-10:])

...    "Call me Ishmael. Some years ago--never mind how long precisely."

code.what_it_does: Prints the vocabulary size, its 10 most and 10 least frequent entries, and the number of tokens produced for the novel's opening sentence. (The printed book glues the fourth >>> prompt to the end of the previous output line; it is restored to its own line here.)

line_explanations.explanation: 64 entries: 63 distinct lowercase characters plus [UNK]; the cap of 100 was not reached.
Most frequent first: [UNK] (forced to index 0), then space, e, t, a, o, n, i, s, h, roughly the classic English letter-frequency order.
Least frequent kept characters: rare symbols @ $ % # = ~ & + < >.
Tokenizes "Call me Ishmael. Some years ago--never mind how long precisely." and prints its length: 63, one token per character, spaces and punctuation included.

code.algorithm: Inspection of dict insertion order and a tokenizer call.
code.theory_link: Evidence for the character tokenizer's small vocabulary and long sequences (p.414).
pitfalls: A real REPL would print lists with single quotes.
The 63 counts the original sentence's characters; lowercasing does not change the length.

# AI-written illustration (not from the book)
line = "Call me Ishmael. Some years ago--never mind how long precisely."
print(len(line))                    # 63 characters

deeper.title: Character vs. word length of the opening line
deeper.body:
For "Call me Ishmael. Some years ago--never mind how long precisely.":

- characters: **63** (printed on this page);
- word-regex tokens: call, me, ishmael, ., some, years, ago, never, mind, how, long, precisely, . = **13** (the "--" is dropped because "-" is not in the regex).

That is about 4.8x compression for words. The word count was computed for these notes; p.414 prints the book's own word-tokenizer result.

deeper.title: Reading corpus statistics from the vocabulary
deeper.body: Because tokens are inserted in frequency order and Python dicts keep insertion order, `list(vocabulary.keys())` is a ranked frequency list. The head (space, e, t, a, o, ...) reflects English letter frequencies; space comes first because roughly one character in five or six is a space. The tail (@, $, %, #, ...) is noise-like material, likely from the e-book's license and header boilerplate. This is a quick sanity check on any tokenizer you build.

misconceptions.claim: With max_size=100 the character vocabulary has 100 entries.
misconceptions.correction: It has 64, because the lowercased novel only contains 63 distinct (non-newline) characters; max_size is an upper bound.

misconceptions.claim: Vocabulary indices are arbitrary in these listings.
misconceptions.correction: They are frequency ranks: index 1 is the most common token (space), and the last indices are the rarest symbols.

misconceptions.claim: A small vocabulary means short encodings.
misconceptions.correction: The opposite holds: the 64-entry character vocabulary encodes a 63-character line as 63 tokens. The word tokenizer has a larger vocabulary but shorter sequences (p.414).

questions.question: Why is the character vocabulary length 64 rather than 100?
options: compute_char_vocabulary drops the 36 least common characters
Only 63 distinct lowercase characters occur in the text, plus [UNK]
questions.answer: Only 63 distinct lowercase characters occur in the text, plus [UNK]
questions.explanation: most_common(99) returns at most as many items as there are distinct tokens. Nothing is dropped below the cap, max_size is respected, and Keras plays no role in the vocabulary function.

questions.question: What is the single change from Listing 14.2 to Listing 14.4 (apart from variable names)?
questions.answer: The split regex: r"[\w]+|[.,!?;]" instead of r".".
questions.explanation: The page says "We can also substitute this new split rule into our vocabulary function."

questions.question: Why are the first entries of the vocabulary [UNK], space, e, t, a, o, ...?
questions.answer: [UNK] is placed at index 0 by construction; the rest are appended in descending frequency from most_common, and in English text the space and letters e, t, a, o are the most frequent characters.
questions.explanation: Dict insertion order preserves that ranking when listing keys.

questions.question: The opening line has 63 characters and becomes 63 character tokens. If a word tokenizer produced 13 tokens for it, what is the compression ratio, and roughly how many characters per word-token is that?
questions.answer: 63 / 13 is about 4.8, so roughly 4.8 characters per word token (spaces included).
questions.explanation: Sequence length shrinks by the average number of characters each word token stands for. The 13 comes from applying the word regex in these notes; check p.414 for the book's printed result.

questions.question: What does keras.utils.get_file return in this code?
options: The text contents of the file
The local path to the downloaded (cached) file
questions.answer: The local path to the downloaded (cached) file
questions.explanation: The result is passed to open(filename, "r"), so it is a path. The list of lines comes from list(open(...)), and no Dataset is created.

questions.question: What would happen if you passed a vocabulary built by compute_char_vocabulary to WordTokenizer?
questions.answer: Almost every word token would be missing from the character vocabulary and map to [UNK] (only single-letter words and the punctuation marks would match), making the encoding useless.
questions.explanation: The vocabulary must be built with the same split rule as the tokenizer, which is why Listing 14.4 exists.

questions.question: Predict, before reading p.414, how the word-level vocabulary size and sequence length for Moby Dick will compare with the character-level results here.
questions.answer: A much larger vocabulary (thousands of words; it fills a 2,000 cap, and about 17,000 would be needed for the whole book) but much shorter sequences.
questions.explanation: This is exactly the comparison drawn on p.414.
